#3771. After days of controversy, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has resigned

Nvidia's founder and CEO Jensen Huang has resigned from his position as leader of one of the most valuable companies in the world.

After days mired in controversy, which began amid reports of Huang's alleged affair with a Chinese spy, Nvidia has announced Huang's resignation as company president, chief executive officer, and board member, effective immediately. Finance chief Colette Kress will take over as interim CEO and will remain in the position until a permanent CEO is chosen.

"Colette has helped lead Nvidia through a period of extraordinary growth and has a deep understanding of our business, customers, operations and financial position," Harvey Jones, chair of Nvidia's board of directors wrote in a statement accompanying the news. "She is supported by an experienced leadership team that has been instrumental in executing Nvidia's strategy and advancing its technology roadmap. The Board has full confidence in Colette and the leadership team, and we expect the company's operations, customer commitments and product roadmap to continue without interruption."

Kress, in the same announcement, says she intends to build on the foundation laid by Huang over the past 33 years, and "continue advancing the work that has made Nvidia a leader in accelerated computing and AI, and execute on the opportunities ahead." Perhaps unsurprisingly, there's no mention of gaming graphics cards in there.

Nvidia's announcement ends by thanking Huang for his time at the company: "Jensen’s contributions to Nvidia are profound. Nvidia is one of the most consequential technology companies in the world. The Board and the company thank Jensen for his immeasurable contributions to the company and the industry."

Nvidia's board met on Wednesday to decide whether to remove Huang amid allegations he had participated in a second affair, this time with a subordinate, following reports of his alleged affair with a Chinese spy. That initial incident prompted a company-wide apology from Huang and an independent investigation exploring whether he'd been the target of a "foreign intelligence effort".

Nvidia will likely remain under increased scrutiny moving forward. There are particular concerns around the company's chips being imported to China despite trade bans.

After a decade and change, Grand Theft Auto VI finally drops this week. Not just one of the most overwhelmingly anticipated games in years, but a hard stress test for a future without physical media. With days left, players who picked up advance retail copies are reporting issues with the download code inside. These range from the codes being claimed in advance or missing entirely.

“Can you imagine the excitement of receiving GTA VI, after having pre-ordered it weeks ago, only for it to arrive without the code?” posted McKuin, who seems to be having this exact problem.

Puedes imaginar la ilusiÃ³n de recibir el GTA VI despuÃ©s de reservarlo hace semanas y que te llegue sin el cÃ³digo. (No es un cÃ³digo que se raspa literalmente viene impreso asÃ­)@SoyAlexWhite #rockstargames #playstation #GTA6 #gtaiv pic.twitter.com/eXfEsGkB1a

Last week, excited Grand Theft Auto players could pick up “physical copies” ahead of launch. While the boxes contain no disc, they do contain a code that would enable the console to preload the game for that magical day. Over the last 24 hours, grievances about the codes have spread across social media, assuming thereâs even a code to speak of.

Within the lining of the gameâs cover sheet is a grey, patterned line where the code is meant to be. While it resembles a scratch-off strip, the code is simply printed on top. As certain players report their codes to be claimed in advance, some theorize itâs possible to shine a hard light at the side of the box, potentially revealing the code without it ever leaving the store. That said, our own editor-in-chief attempted to recreate this trick on his copy to no avail. Other members of the press are experiencing the same. Some believe that international copies, especially those in PAL regions, may have been packaged differently. But this is a speculation layered on top of another speculation. Like all hearsay about Grand Theft Auto it demands a chunky grain of salt.

More believable, and arguably more devastating, are players who are claiming their copy arrived without any code at all. This is a woe that weâve seen before, requiring little more than a printer having an off-moment. Eons ago a couple copies of Batman: Arkham City arrived without their dedicated DLC codes, but that only locked out the Catwoman prologue. Now those who have paid full price, in advance, get nothing. A gut punch and an omen of how small mishaps can devastate harder in a world without physical media.

Numerous images and videos of people with code-less boxes have emerged on platforms like Reddit and X, with others claiming theyâve been refused refunds or stonewalled by Rockstarâs support line. That said, the rumor milling around Grand Theft Auto is a cottage industry in and of itself. Always flex your skepticism on this subject matter. The ‘light trick’ explanation feels like a bit of a yarn, but potential misprints are well within the realm of possibility.

We have reached out to Rockstar for comment.

When World of Warcraft: Forever's beta first launched, I lamented its long stretches of silence and penchant for ambience over theatrics. I still sort of stand by that, but after spending more time in Azeroth (and discovering the loop music setting) I've a new-found appreciation for both WoW's soundtrack and ambient music as a whole.

It's also got me thinking about what makes a soundtrack ambient versus something more melodic. I'm chronically Final Fantasy 14-brained, where just about everything has a grand thematic soundtrack to it—the jauntiness of the Gold Saucer, the soothing Middle-earthness of Gridania's outer Shroud zones, the grand organs of Ishgard's bitterly cold landscape. You can't escape composer Masayoshi Soken's penchant for leifmotifs. He will turn anything into an orchestral spectacle.

I'm a big JRPG fan in general, a genre I think is the absolute master of thematic soundtracks. But I also think fondly of games I've played over the years that are a little more pared down, their soundtracks there for a little atmosphere rather than actively driving the narrative. Minecraft's OST is a masterclass in ambience, and is in regular rotation across my videogame-themed Spotify playlists. I also have a huge soft spot for the soundtrack behind Mirror's Edge—one which settles in this almost otherworldly ambiance, only ramping up when Faith is in a perilous situation.

But what about you? Do you prefer the more subtle nuances that an atmospheric soundtrack has to offer? Or do you like your videogame music loud, in your face, and full of dramatics? Be sure to leave a comment and let me know which one's your favourite and why.

#3768. As low-effort AI slop continues to flood Steam, yet more developers announce game delays caused by Valve's growing approval backlog

"There's no outcome of this that allows Valve neutrality on AI".

More indie developers say they've been forced to delay the impending release of their games as a result of Steam's growing approvals backlog - a relatively recent problem that's believed to stem from an influx of AI slop on the platform.

Earlier this month, developers began complaining about delays to Valve's approval process, which was extending the time it took to get their games published on Steam. Valve responded, explaining approval times could now take up to 12 days, due to the number of submissions it was having to re-review. One week on, the situation doesn't seem to have improved.

New turn-based tower defence game Australia Did It: End-of-the-World Railway Defense Business, co-developed by acclaimed indie designer Rami Ismail and Aesthetician Labs, was previously set for release on 10th November. Unfortunately, the game has now been delayed while the wait continues for Valve to review the latest build.

"We're still waiting for Steam to give us the final greenlight and finish their build review process," publisher Mystic Forge wrote on the Steam forums. "We have been stuck waiting for it for a few weeks now and unfortunately we just don't know when they will get around to reviewing it at this point."

Speaking to Eurogamer, Ismail added that Australia Did It has been in Steam's approval queue for much longer than he's used to: "We've been in the queue since 20th October, failed over a minor controller input issue on 5th November (which we resolved the same day), and we've been waiting again since with no meaningful response from Valve despite follow-ups."

"I'm used to hold-and-wait patterns on console," Ismail continued, "but Steam has historically been much more snappy - 10-14 days pre-launch was usually enough to fail twice and still ship on time," he added.

Amazing Slot Survivor (A.S.S.), the debut title from TwoMenGames, is facing similar issues, and has had to retract its release date announcement after being stuck in Steam's approval queue. Amazing Slot Survivor, which adds a slot machine spin to the bullet heaven auto-shooting genre, was initially set for release on 13th November.

"Steam's review process for the release is taking longer than we expected," TwoMenGames wrote in a message on Steam. "We know many of you have been counting on the schedule we announced earlier, and we are very sorry to bring you this [postponement] news instead of the good news you were hoping for." Amazing Slot Survivor's demo, which was previously set to disappear with the game's full release, has returned to Steam until the developer announces a new launch date.

These are far from the only examples, and a cursory look on social media reveals many more indie games are affected by the problem, including the likes of Bottled by Bears, and Food Devils.

Valve recently attempted to address the delays its facing by introducing stricter submission guidelines designed to stop the lowest-effort games, such as those vibe-coded entirely with gen-AI, from joining its approval queue. However, Ismail doesn't think that's good enough.

"I am concerned that Valve trying to avoid taking a political position on AI is forcing them into choices that will inevitably be worse for developers," he told Eurogamer. "If sloppers can submit several game clones a day through automated systems, the only way for Valve to stem the tide of games damaging genuine developers' work is to put constraints on game distribution, increase fees, or make the process more complicated.

"In the 'open market' Valve seems to so adore, they're going to be the ones carrying the costs for moderation, so I don't think they'll like the open market on this - but there's no outcome of this that allows Valve neutrality on AI and not do things that will ultimately make life worse for genuine developers," he added.

Spoilers for Avengers Endgame: Encore’s new scenes lie ahead.

September marked the release of Avengers Endgame: Encore, an extended version of Marvel Studios’ 2019 culmination film. Aside from getting the chance to see the superhero spectacle on the big screen again, fans were hyped by the inclusion of four scenes that would have ties to the upcoming Avengers: Doomsday. Unfortunately, those Encore moments leaked early and sparked early speculation. Now, the film is available to stream with a Disney+ subscription and, with that, I went ahead and pulled the timestamps.

Fans should know that the first of these four new scenes begins at the 2:48:50 mark and is an extension of the original film’s closing scene. Many will probably remember that the OG cut of the film ends with Steve Rogers (Captain America) reuniting with his former love, Peggy Carter, and enjoying domestic bliss. The extended scene adds an interesting twist to the proceedings, as after the two share their kiss, there’s a knock at their door. While Steve hides, Peggy answers, and the visitor is revealed to be none other than Loki.

Peggy asks the former God of Mischief if she can help him, leading him to say, ‘No, but I believe I can help you. Both of you.” From there, a shocked Steve – recognizing his former foe’s voice – reveals himself, and the scene cuts to black. While there’s not too much to go off, at the very least, I can imagine this tees off Steve’s return in Doomsday.

The second new scene starts around 2:53:47 and shifts the focus to Dr. Bruce Banner. At this point, the tormented scientist is held up in an underground military complex following his (Jean Grey-induced) rampage in Spider-Man: Brand New Day. Banner is in the middle of recording a video journal about his circumstances and plan to suppress his gamma radiation. In a shocking turn, Doctor Doom (who remains unseen) appears before Banner and says he’s arrived to collect him. The scene ends with the sound of the Hulk’s roar.

Doomsday directors Joe and Anthony Russo discussed this Banner scene, and they remained very coy about its implications. At the very least, though, Joe did say that Doom’s “interest may extend beyond just Banner.”

Yes, the TVA (introduced in Loki) makes it return during the third additional scene – which drops at the 2:56:30 mark – in Endgame: Encore, though it’s not exactly an ideal situation for the characters. Mobius M. Mobius arrives at work, where he meets up with colleagues Ouroboros and Casey. It’s there that they and their colleagues witness countless multiversal incursions in real time, much to their horror. With that, OB declares the multiverse is collapsing.

The very end of OG Endgame’s closing credits features a series of “ting” sounds, which were – at the time – said to be paying homage to Tony Stark forging the Mark I in Iron Man. In Encore, this starts around the 3:04:30 mark, and there’s a very different reason for it. After the sounds are heard, the screen eventually flashes to some quick shots of Victor von Doom forging his infamous mask.

While some may take issue with MCU scenes of such “great… importance” happening in this alternate cut, but they are still important for what’s to come nonetheless. I – like so many others, am curious as to how this is all going to pay off. Let’s hope these plot threads come together in a cohesive way so that when Avengers: Doomsday arrives on December 18 amid the 2026 movie schedule, everything makes sense. In the meantime, though, take these timestamps and stream the new scenes from Encore for yourself.

#3764. World of Warcraft: Forever players in Australia and New Zealand are struggling to get sunlight, and not for the usual MMO reasons

World of Warcraft: Forever players are having a blast in the new MMO, but not everyone is basking in the rays of its successful launch. Players located in Australia, New Zealand, and other Oceania countries are having a bit of a sunlight problem.

But it's not that too much time behind the computer is keeping WoW players on the other side of the globe away from their precious Vitamin D. Rather, it's in-game sunlight that's scarce for our Oceania friends.

World of Warcraft: Forever, if you didn't already known, has a lovely in-game day/night cycle that aligns with your server clock rather than your local time. So, for a British player, the server time is one hour ahead of GMT. That means if I play during the day I see the sun hanging over Azeroth, and if I do a late night MMO session it's replaced by the moon.

However, while Oceania players can access a data centre in Australia that allows for a solid connection to WoW, they still share the same mega-servers with North Americans. That mega-server is aligned with North American time, differing drastically from Oceania time zones. In other words, for World of Warcraft: Forever players in Oceania, day is night and night is day. And they've had enough!

Reddit user Playful_Artichoke981 has been at the forefront of requests asking Blizzard to address the problem , though they're far from alone. Currently, Oceania players see full daylight in-game from around midnight to 6am in the morning, which obviously is far from normal gaming hours for the majority of players in the region.

"We don't hate the nighttime. We just want variety," writes Playful_Artichoke981. "We don't want to have to compromise our sleep schedules to experience this game in all its glory." Another user, cuddlegoop, echoes the sentiment: "I am totally fine with my day/night changing when I join an NA party. Just let me see the sun! I was up late last night and the view over the bay at Shadowfan Keep in the dawn was so beautiful I want to see stuff like that more often."

Eurogamer has contacted Blizzard to ask if it has plans to address the issue, but we've not received a response at the time of writing.

World of Warcraft: Forever is proving exceptionally popular, breaking records as the biggest launch in the series' history. And based on what I've played this week, it's looking to be a brilliant MMO that's well worth jumping into, if you have the time.

Miniature designer and artist Aly Morrison has died, as confirmed by Trish Carden Miniatures and Design on Facebook. Carden, Morrison's ex-wife and former partner in Marauder Miniatures, posted that, "Mharaid and I are heartbroken to announce the passing of Aly Morrison, a very much loved father, veteran wargames miniatures designer and friend to many around the tabletop and the world. Aly passed unexpectedly but peacefully this Wednesday, and will be sorely missed."

Aly Morrison began sculpting for Citadel in 1983 as a freelancer before joining the studio full-time in 1986. He and Trish were then made stewards of Games Workshop's imprint Marauder Miniatures in 1988, where they had free reign to create quirky and characterful figures like the mohawked dwarf trollslayers and the giant with a whaler's beard and a booze barrel strapped to his waist that became archetypal parts of Warhammer.

Morrison also crafted the first miniatures for Blood Bowl players and drew the tokens to represent them in the board game's first edition. During his time at Games Workshop every faction from dark elves to space marines eventually benefited from his touch.

He's also well-regarded as a painter, and his reliance on a dark wash with a hint of purple in it jokingly known as "Aly's Brown Liquid" was legendary. He continued working on the recipe over the years, with a recent iteration described on his blog in 2020 if you want to whip some up yourself.

Though Marauder was eventually folded back into Citadel, Morrison continued at Games Workshop until his retirement earlier this year. The company remembered him by saying, "Aly’s kindness and generosity as a mentor have left an indelible mark on the Warhammer Studio. Humble, magnanimous and with an incorrigible wit, to sit beside Aly and hear his wisdom and love of Warhammer miniatures design, was to be in the presence of a master. No matter your level of experience, he always had something insightful to add, to help make the creation 'more Warhammer'."

#3761. Xbox boss seemingly champions gen-AI development as she celebrates 25 years of Xbox: "A small team will be able to build worlds that today demand hundreds of developers"

Xbox leader Asha Sharma has alluded to harnessing the power of generative AI when making games, in a memo published this afternoon.

The memo, titled 25 years of Xbox, charts the growth of Microsoft from small beginnings through to the thousands-strong company it is today. But it's Sharma's comments at the end of the memo that are of particular interest.

While talking about what the next 25 years could bring, Sharma lamented that "too many ideas never become games" and that "too many games fall short of what their creators imagined". "For decades, this has been the unavoidable tradeoff of ambition," she wrote. "We must change this."

Sharma continued: "Throughout human history, the scale of what we could create was determined by the people, capital, and resources we could command. That relationship is beginning to break. A single person will soon be able to wield capabilities that once required entire nations. A small team will be able to build worlds that today demand hundreds of developers and hundreds of millions of dollars. And our largest studios will be able to pursue ambitions as far beyond today's games as Microsoft Flight Simulator 2024 is from its first entry in 1982."

There is no explicit mention of generative AI here, but the language is suggestive - "a single person will soon be able to wield capabilities that once required entire nations". Furthermore, Asha's memo follows last month's announcement of an Xbox Labs initiative that also sounded like it was based around generative AI, despite avoiding the phrase specifically.

This isn't a surprise, of course. Microsoft as a wider company is all-in on generative AI, with Copilot, and Sharma's background at Microsoft is in AI. But it's an area she's avoided speaking too enthusiastically about since her hiring as Xbox boss earlier this year. At the time, Sharma said she has "no tolerance for bad AI", and there's been such a lot else going on in the months since - including wide-ranging restructuring resulting in the loss of thousands of Xbox jobs - that the topic of generative AI has fallen into the background. Perhaps now we're seeing the sprouting seeds of it.

One of the most thoughtful sketches SNL has given us in a long time.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

SNL is best known for its irreverent characters and sharp political commentary, but some of the best sketches in the history of the show are ones that make pointed observations about society. Think Mom Jeans or Meet Your Second Wife. We got another one of those bangers last night, and many fans felt so heard they weren’t sure if they could even laugh.

The sketch in question is a fake commercial for an elder care service called Sister. It recommends that instead of putting your loved one in a nursing home or spending thousands a week on professional care, you instead simply text your sister. She’ll drop everything in her life to come help while you continue to live your life as if there’s not a family crisis going on.

Normally when SNL drops a sketch on social, all of the top comments are about exactly what you would expect. They’re messages about how it is or isn’t funny. They’re observations about who is good in the sketch and who isn’t good in the sketch. That’s not the case with this one. Instead, a majority of the comments on multiple platforms are about how the commentator either feels seen or feels called out. There are comments with first person stories and comments saying their real life is exactly what the woman in the sketch is going through.

The top comment on YouTube already has more than eleven hundred likes and pretty much tells the whole story…

Other popular comments on YouTube included one woman saying she almost had “a stroke from rage” while watching. Several said they were going to use the sketch to have a conversation with their siblings because they felt heard. It was the same pattern on X too. A woman who works as an estate attorney said it’s “not funny” because it’s so accurate to what she sees every day. Others commented saying the part about the siblings who did nothing still getting an inheritance felt especially powerful since that was their real life experience. Others just commented the classic, "WTF?"

To me, this sketch is Saturday Night Live at its absolute best. I’m not saying we need this level of pointed middle fingers all the time, but it feels especially meaningful when the show gives voice to a problem or frustrating dynamic in society that isn’t often commented on. Caretakers are an underseen and underheard from group in American society, and you can tell by all the big reactions to this sketch that they’re happy to feel heard.

A strong case could be made that this week’s Saturday Night Live episode was the best of the season. Guest host John Mulaney really delivered a ton of dynamite sketches that covered a lot of territory. In addition to this little slice of brilliance, we also got a musical about central park horses, a middle finger toward boomers who betrayed the principles of Woodstock and some fun character work. Even Weekend Update was a banger and included a fantastic joke about Colin Jost’s doomed ferry boat.

SNL is off for awhile, but the show will return after Thanksgiving with guest host Amanda Seyfried, who should be spectacular in a very different way than Mulaney. I can’t wait.

BioWareElectronic ArtsMass EffectMass Effect 3

Since EA made the decision to shutter Mass Effect creators BioWare, effectively ending the series, fans have launched an intense campaign to save the beloved sci-fi saga. So far theyâve deployed petitions, billboards, banner trucks and video reunions. This week, pulling a page from a previous protest over the third gameâs ending, theyâre trying a new tactic: Cupcakes.

Alongside @kalaelizabeth, we sent N7 cupcakes to EA's HQ for #SaveMassEffect!

In 2012, fans sent cupcakes to BioWare over ME3's endings. We're echoing that gesture with a different message, using peaceful, creative ways to make our voices heard. pic.twitter.com/xXy9x1vjdk

— We are Mass Effect – #SaveMassEffect (@WeAreMassEffect) November 13, 2026

On Friday, illustrator Kala Elizabeth and other “Save Mass Effect” organizers arranged to have a batch of N7 decorated cupcakes sent to EAâs Redwood City headquarters. While gifting tasty baked goods to express outrage seems a little odd, the play is an homage to a similar campaign from 2012, when fans were angered by Mass Effect 3âs infamous endings. That movement, calling themselves “Retake Mass Effect,” took umbrage with the differing paths all ultimately funneling towards similar, lackluster conclusions. Poking fun, fans sent the studio 400 cupcakes, each decorated with red, green and blue icing, but tasting exactly the same on the inside.

While it wasnât limited to cupcakes alone, the 2012 movement was somewhat successful. BioWare agreed to release DLC later that year that expanded upon the ending choices. While the resolution remained controversial, it delivered a loud message to fans eager to change trajectory. BioWare, not needing that many cupcakes at the time, sent the desserts to a local youth shelter.

“The delivery person was asked quite a few questions by EA staff at reception, who told her they were very much aware of the #SaveMassEffect movement,” posted the WeAreMassEffect account. “Despite this, the reception staff accepted the cupcakes.”

This time around, fans only cooked up a dozen cupcakes. Given the stakes of this fight, no amount of treats are likely to move the needle. After years of tension between the studio and publisher, EA closed BioWare in October. This was shortly after being acquired by a consortium of private equity firms, including the Saudi Arabia Public Investment Fund and Jared Kushnerâs Affinity Partners. The key reason is reportedly to rally resources around safer bets like Star Wars tie-ins.

The unspectacular end of BioWare and its games has cut deep for fans, who are hoping to reverse course at some level, improbable as that may be. Its major fronts are a public petition, which has received over a quarter million signatures, and sympathies from the Canadian New Democratic Party, whose leadership has used the untimely fate of the Edmonton-based developer to lobby for stronger labor protections against private equity.

The preview version of SteamOS 3.10.0 has just dropped, and with it comes better support for AMD and Nvidia hardware, and it's now based on Linux kernel 7.3.

For AMD graphics, the latest SteamOS update adds support for HDMI 2.1 VRR (Variable Refresh Rate), FRL(Fixed Rate Link), and ALLM (Auto Low Latency Mode). This should all contribute to a smoother gaming experience with higher bandwidth video and less input lag.

As for Nvidia graphics, it has reportedly received increased stability and performance, alongside support for Mesh Shaders on Turing and newer architectures. The latest SteamOS updates also fixed rendering corruption issues in Shadow of the Tomb Raider and The Surge 2.

Then, of course, SteamOS now uses the Linux 7.3 kernel (which launched last month).

Those are the big updates from SteamOS 3.10.0, but there are also a handful of fixes and changes. Game Mode has had the following changes:

SteamOS Previews are experimental by nature. You have to swap your update channel in Steam settings to get access, and there's always a chance new updates come with bugs or stability problems. If you come across a problem, Valve has a form to track SteamOS bugs.

If you don't fancy downloading a preview, SteamOS 3.10.0 is likely to come to the public channel at some point in the future, based on feedback from the preview.

#3754. Will GTA 6 break the internet? UK broadband operator braces for impact, saying "GTA 6 has been on our radar for a long time"

"We'll be watching for a new download record."

As Grand Theft Auto 6 breaks pre-order records on the PlayStation and Xbox stores, and looks poised to break many more sales records once it launches next week, questions of whether it will also break the internet arise. Collective network load will undoubtedly spike around its release - will regional infrastructure be able to bear it?

Major game releases register nationally for broadband use: we know this from an investigation into gaming downloads and how much they cost the environment we published in 2021. We also know that UK communications regulator Ofcom negotiates with gaming companies to try and avoid major game launches happening alongside major cultural occasions, such as sporting events, which are likely to spike broadband use. The network pipes can be clogged, and there's arguably never been a game as anticipated as GTA 6 to clog them.

For this reason, Openreach - the company that runs the largest broadband network in the UK - has been tracking Rockstar's latest game closely. "GTA 6 has been on our radar for a long time," Trevor Linney, Openreach's director for network technology, told Eurogamer. "We know from games like Fortnite and Call of Duty that a major release or update can drive huge amounts of data across the network, so it'll be fascinating to see just how much GTA moves the needle. Our network and teams are ready, and GTA 6 is certainly one we'll be watching for a new download record."

A spokesperson for Ofcom, meanwhile, said: "Broadband networks should be well placed to handle this download. Ofcom's Broadband Code of Practice means providers must give customers clear, realistic information and guarantee a minimum speed. If you’re not getting this, you may be able to leave your contract penalty-free. Check your speed now, so you can focus on the game rather than the loading screen." Ofcom has a website with sections devoted to broadband speeds and changing providers, in case you're interested.

Alongside yesterday's announcements that GTA 6 had become the most pre-ordered game in Xbox Store and PlayStation Store history, Sony and Microsoft shared strongly worded advice that players download the game ahead of time to avoid complications caused by "unprecedented demand". We saw last year what happened when Hollow Knight: Silksong arrived, causing chaos on Xbox, Steam, and Nintendo servers, and that game's reach was an order of magnitude less than GTA 6's. I don't recall a Selfridges store takeover in London for Silksong - do you?

#3753. Halifax Parents Hoping To Reverse Nine-Year-Old’s $20,000 Roblox Bill

Ever since video games entered the family home, so began the eternal schism between confused parents and the most popular software. PokÃ©mon. Grand Theft Auto. Which one is Zelda anyway. It never ends. But only in recent history has this generational divide begun to carry an unsuspecting price tag. A Halifax couple were stunned to discover that their nine-year-old son racked up tens of thousands in fees while gaming. Though successful in reversing the charges from most parties, Roblox remains a holdout, where the kid managed to spend $20 grand.

“He enters buttons and ta-da,” says mother Dawn Sutherland (no relation to the other, Canadian Don Sutherland). “He has no clue that he has spent any money.”

According to CTV News, Nova Scotians Carey Chernoff and Dawn Sutherland were unaware of the massive tab their son had accrued over a summer of gaming. Each member of the household has their own iPad, but each is linked to a shared Apple Pay account. After receiving an alert that their Mastercard was maxed out, the parents discovered their son had spent $28,000 (roughly $19,000 USD) through in-game purchases. They say that upon asking to be refunded, most of the gaming companies complied, with the exception of one. With the lionâs share of the bill, the two are hoping Roblox will be more reasonable.

In a statement to CTV, Roblox said that “These purchases were made via a third party. We encourage the family to reach out to the merchant for review of the transactions.” The implied third party could be Apple, who did not respond to CTV’s request for comment.

“It so easily can happen to anyone,” says Sutherland. “It terrifies most parents.”

Itâs an increasingly common story. In fact, itâs not even the only Roblox spending scandal on CTV in recent history. The sum does leave a bigger dent than most others, however. And while Roblox does offer parental controls, including those around spending limits, itâs clear that these features arenât incredibly well communicated among the public.

Though older than most of its user base, Roblox is immensely popular among young children. The responsibility that comes with maintaining an adolescent demographic has rarely been met by the company, and their responses to criticism leaves much to be desired. While parents should better monitor their childrenâs media and gaming habits, thereâs also plenty of room for better policy on in-game spending. Around the globe, consumer protection bureaus have begun to target long-running monetization practices, though these policy trends are typically slower-moving in North America.

#3750. Xbox boss announces Wolfenstein 3 and confirms new game in development at idSoftware despite reported job cut "bloodbath"

"One of gaming's most important franchises".

Xbox boss Asha Sharma has confirmed Wolfenstein 3 is in development at MachineGames, the Swedish studio behind the acclaimed Wolfenstein: The New Order, Wolfenstein 2: The New Colossal, and 2024's celebrated Indiana Jones and the Great Circle. Additionally, she revealed Doom developer idSoftware - one of the Microsoft-owned studios heavily impacted by sweeping Xbox job cuts earlier this year - is now working on a new game.

Sharma has, of course, been on a bit of a PR offensive of late, positioning herself alongside snippets of positive news at a time Xbox is embroiled in a massive business "reset" effort that has resulted in proposed studio closures and mass layoffs that will ultimately see 3,200 Xbox employees lose their jobs. This week's Wolfenstein 3 reveal similarly arrived in the form of a tweet posted directly from her social media account.

"Wolfenstein 3 is officially in production at MachineGames," Sharma wrote on X. "One of gaming's most important franchises, and a team that has done remarkable work bringing it forward. Looking forward to sharing more." As for idSoftware's new project, confirmation of that - again attributed directly to Sharma - appeared in a post on Bethesda's website. "Slaughter Mode comes to Doom: The Dark Ages - Revelations on Monday," she wrote, "and the team is already working on its next game."

In July, sweeping job cuts at Xbox resulted in 96 of idSoftware's 136 employees being laid off in a move one former team member described as a "bloodbath". Since then, idSoftware co-studio director Marty Stratton has attempted to downplay the cuts, recently insisting the studio was "doing great". He added id was "working more closely than ever" with MachineGames - a studio which appears to have escaped Sharma's restructuring efforts so far.

This week's Wolfenstein and idSoftware news follows similar efforts by Xbox to reassure fans their favourite franchises are unaffected by the recent layoffs. Shortly after substantial job cuts at Bethesda were confirmed, the company moved to insist The Elder Scrolls 6 was still "on the way" and that its plans were "unaffected" (the company has since released a trailer announcing its subtitle). It also confirmed a new Fallout game was in development.

Xbox's year of bad news - which includes ongoing boycott efforts relating to Microsoft's controversial involvement with the Israeli military - comes as the division celebrates its 25th anniversary. Earlier this week, Sharma shared a memo to staff marking the occasion, albeit one in which she seemingly championed a gen-AI future for games development, enthusing that, "A small team will be able to build worlds that today demand hundreds of developers".

My position on the debate is fairly neutral—I think you could maybe bump up the mob XP by around 10% as a compromise—but overall I think they're fine. The new ones are bangers, and I get a huge bunch of XP from doing them at least once. Blizzard's recent choices, however, did have me scratching my head over the weekend.

For a short time, via a hotfix, enemies in dungeons wouldn't give experience points to anyone in the group if they were trivial (that is, greyed out) to at least one party member. On paper, this sounds incredibly reasonable. WoW has suffered from a plague of dungeon boosters (that is, people selling runs of dungeons to let folks AFK through their levelling journey) particularly in Classic.

But the moment you take a second to stare at how Classic dungeons are designed, you start to see the cracks form. Uldaman, for instance, has a level range of 41-51 in my dungeon finder. Maraudon, 46-55. Then there's the issue of the Scarlet Monastery, whose entire gauntlet runs from level 30 to 44 and is often done in one big sweep by groups.

In other words, it was possible to be maybe a couple levels over the recommended range for a dungeon—which is certainly a great help, but I don't think can be counted as a boost—and ruin the already-diminished XP gains for everyone. Which is counter-intuitive in a game that's meant to be social.

To Blizzard's credit, its devs did spring into action on Saturday, amending the hotfix: "Yesterday, we updated dungeon play so that experience granted by an enemy in an instance is nullified if a high level player is in the group and enemy is trivial to that player. For some dungeons, the new restriction missed the mark because of the overall level range of the enemies in the dungeon.

"With hotfixes that are now live, we’ve just deployed a further change to this restriction, making it so that the XP nullification only kicks in when the high-level player is more than 12 levels above the level of the enemies."

To me that's more than reasonable. I don't think, say, a level 25 character coming to help their mate out with Deadmines should be ruining the XP gains for everybody else—sure, their presence makes the dungeon a heck of a lot easier, but so does grouping up for quests in the open world. 12 levels seems a fair compromise.

#3747. Universal Paperclips Creator Blends Scrabble And Strategy In Towers Of Babble

They say the pen is mightier than the sword but so far in this life of mine I have yet to kick someoneâs ass with a Google Doc. If you fantasize about twisting your affinity for words into more traditional combat, the creator of Universal Paperclips has just the game for you. Blending together the fundamentals of Scrabble, tower defense strategy games and some roguelike seasoning, Towers of Babble is perfect for the logophile looking for a more bespoke Scribblenauts.

Each campaign in Towers of Babble begins with a handful of letter tiles. Spell a noun and you can build a unit on the map. Like larvae in an anthill, words are predeterminedly assigned to harvesters or defensive units. Spell out verbs and modifiers to create power-ups for your nouns. Use your harvested resources to purchase upgrades, such as a larger selection of tiles or adding premium stats to certain letters. Survive enough waves of enemies and youâll have conquered the level, itself assigned to a new word, and can carry over certain elements to your next struggle session.

Created by alternative indie dev Frank Lantz, best known for the absurdist industrial simulator Universal Paperclips, Towers of Babble boasts 120,000 levels and some 200,000 word units to choose from. Many words have loose affiliations to their definitions. The semiotics conjure its own form of magic, imbuing units with healing elements, poison clouds of chip damage, stronger shields, bigger blasting super missiles. Compounding words together into long-winded, Germanic strings of nonsense. While each “Librarian” plays alone, they fight this war together. Each conquered word contributes to the same massive tower. What happens when each is cleared, and this lexicon reaches the heavens, is anyoneâs guess.

#3746. Slay the Spire 2 gets its first new character since its massively successful launch in March as part of "biggest" beta patch yet

Slay the Spire 2, which released into early access earlier this year, is expanding once more with a major new beta update. This introduces the deckbuilder's first new character since launch - a whimsical musician armed with a bow - alongside two new modes, and more.

When Slay the Spire 2 arrived back in March, it was to much enthusiastic acclaim. Eurogamer's Bertie Purchie is a big fan, and has trumpeted its successes on multiple occasions, calling the sequel's co-op mode "transformative". And it was a commercial hit too, managing to shift over 5m copies in just a month of release. All of which means there are plenty of eyes on Slay the Spire 2, eager to see what developer MegaCrit does next.

So far major updates have brought the likes of buffs, balance adjustments, art updates, UI improvements, bug fixes, and more - and MegaCrit has also made other substantial adjustments including the jettisoning of third act boss Doormaker, after it decided the encounter was overly complex. And now, as 2026 nears its conclusion, the studio has released its "biggest (beta) patch yet", including a sweep of major additions.

As per MegaCrit's v0.113.0 patch notes, the headliner is The Fool; Slay the Spire 2's first new character, who's described as a "silly musician who wields a bow". Unsurprisingly, The Fool doesn't arrive in their final form, and the studio says it expects to make a "great number of content and balance changes" before the character is ready for the main branch.

Accompanying The Fool are two new game modes: Blitz and Dread. Blitz is described as a "condensed and chaotic" mode focused on deckbuilding. Unlocked after completing an Ascension run of any difficulty, it comes with five levels of Ascension shared across all characters. "The Merchant's wares feel a bit off," MegaCrit teases, "the map is gone, and Gold no longer matters??"

If you're looking for a more gruelling challenge, though, there's the "brutally difficult" new Dread mode, designed for players who've reached Ascension 10 on all characters, including The Fool. All ascension modifiers are enabled, according to MegaCrit, while bosses are stronger and buff all enemies found across their Act. And if that's still not enough to get your heart racing, MegaCrit notes curses will also pile up as you climb the Spire.

Beyond the headline stuff, v0.113.0 tweaks rest sites so they appear one floor earlier every act, and that's alongside the usual list of UI changes, art additions, nerfs, balance adjustments, and more. Full patch notes can be found on Steam.

Those players eager to put Slay the Spire 2's latest additions through their paces will need to enable the beta branch by right-clicking on Slay the Spire 2 in their Steam library and navigating to Properties > Game Versions & Betas and selecting 'public-beta' from the dropdown menu. MegaCrit notes the game's main branch has also been updated with all content and changes from the previous beta.

I love Jackie Chan. You love Jackie Chan. We ALL love Jackie Chan. However, I think we sometimes forget when we started loving Jackie Chan.

It's kind of crazy to think, but some people's introduction to Jackie was in the 2010 Karate Kid movie starring Jaden Smith (which I love, by the way). For others, they might have discovered him with Rush Hour (which even Chan himself seemed to not have completely understood). For me though, it all started with 1995’s Rumble in the Bronx, which I just rewatched the other day.

I’ve always loved this film, but honestly, after a rewatch, I don’t think most people remember just what an absolute gem this movie is. So, today, I’m here to remind you.

As a Black dude, I love martial arts movies (honestly, who DOESN’T?). The thing is, I’m usually into SERIOUS martial arts films, like stuff from the Shaw Brothers, JCVD classics like Time Cop, and old Bruce Lee joints. Then, in 1995, a movie came along that had everything I love about martial arts, but it was also funny as hell.

Enter Rumble in the Bronx, which basically changed the whole concept of what a martial arts movie could be for me. Here was a film that wasn’t just martial arts, but was a comedy. It was a film that had a lively cast of characters, such as Uncle Bill Ma (Bill Tung), Elaine (Anita Mui), the wheelchair bound, Danny (Morgan Lam) - who could play a Game Gear with no game inside, and Jackie Chan himself as Keung, a police officer who just wants to attend his uncle’s wedding until trouble arrives.

The fight choreography in this movie is SO GOOD (especially the warehouse fight!), and its humor also lands with the same impact. Rumble in the Bronx wasn’t the first movie I'd seen that mixed martial arts with humor - I did grow up in the age of Turtle Power, mind you - but it was the first that wasn’t based on a comic book that still had this sense of humor. Seriously, watch it again. It's probably funnier than you even remember it being.

I first watched Rumble in the Bronx when I was just a kid, and I seriously hated the villains back then. Well, I'm 43 now, and I STILL hate the villains, which is a true testament to just how awful they are to poor Keung in this film. Yes, the late Marc Akerstream as Tony is the main antagonist, and he's a pretty good villain, but even better is his underling, Angelo, played by stuntman Garvin Cross.

Angelo is a true scumbag who is always getting his ass whooped, but also finds ways to mess with Keung. The “best” scene is when Angelo and others corner Keung in an alley and hit glass bottles at him with a baseball bat, cutting Keung severely. I hated Tony’s henchmen when I was a kid, but this really infuriated me as an adult. It made their ultimate beatdown later on that much sweeter.

Lastly, can I just talk about how great the stunt work is in this film? It's not the craziest stuff in the world (we would see WAY crazier stuff from Chan in earlier films of his, many of which came stateside following the success of RitB), but when I saw his death-defying stunts in RitB - like a huge jump between buildings! - I was hooked.

And I wasn't alone. With the humor, action, and crazy stunt work in Rumble in the Bronx, it's little wonder why this film made Jackie Chan a household name - especially since it's set in “America” (Even though it was filmed in Canada).

However, I think people may have forgotten just how all of it - the humor, the action, the stunts - are just perfect in this movie, and I think you need to rewatch it for yourself just to remember. It's still really that good!

Rich is a Jersey boy, through and through. He graduated from Rutgers University (Go, R.U.!), and thinks the Garden State is the best state in the country. That said, he’ll take Chicago Deep Dish pizza over a New York slice any day of the week. Don’t hate. When he’s not watching his two kids, he’s usually working on a novel, watching vintage movies, or reading some obscure book.

#3743. One week from launch, GTA 6's physical map reportedly leaks online thanks to the £350 collector's edition on show in a UK department store

With less than a week to go before GTA 6's hugely anticipated release, the game's final map - or at least a stylised poster version of it, depicting the state of Leonida's key landmarks - has surfaced online. It was reportedly snapped during Selfridge's sizable GTA 6's takeover, and is seemingly the physical map included in Rockstar's £350 collector's edition.

Fans have been pondering GTA 6's map for some time now, cross-referencing previous map leaks with official trailer footage in an attempt to gain some insight into the major landmarks and regions Rockstar has in store. And while the newly leaked map is far from granular, it does at least appear to confirm Leonida's rough layout and the key locations players can visit this time.

Assuming the map's veracity, it's all rendered in an art style somewhere between mid-century tourism poster and Adult Swim, featuring the phrase "The Goodtime State" up top - a riff on the actual Florida's nickname, The Sunshine State - while Leonida's most notable points of interest are interspersed with cartoon figures.

There's a toking turtle (or possibly a tortoise - I'm no expert), a golfer proudly wearing assless chaps, a flying saucer, and more. I'll spare you the geographic details confirmed on the map in case you want to go in unspoiled. One point of amusement though: the way the map photo is cropped means fans searching for confirmation of an in-game Key West are still none the wiser.

It's not entirely clear where the wonkily angled photo originated from, but prominent Rockstar Games community insider Videotech, who shared the image on social media, suggested it came from a "naughty Selfridges employee" during Selfridges' GTA 6 takeover. The map itself appears to be the "double-Sided souvenir poster with map of Leonida" included in Rockstar's eyewateringly expensive GTA 6 Collector's Edition. This costs £350 and doesn't come with a copy of the game. Or assless chaps, for that matter.

This isn't the first time GTA 6's map - officially said to be twice the size of GTA 5's - has leaked online, although previous leaks have been notably more controversial. Earlier this year, a group calling itself CyberLeek shared unofficial gameplay and map details in the name of what it called "Gamers' Rights". In August, with Netflix's official GTA 6 unveiling looming, the group cashed out nearly £200,000 from its crypto scheme.

Amid all this, Rockstar has been embroiled in legal action after it was accused of union busting following the firing of over 30 employees. The case's conclusion has been delayed until next week, meaning a verdict could arrive just as GTA 6 goes on sale.

Go back to the 2000s and early 2010s and it was absolutely the norm for major game developers to use their own in-house engines. However, with games increasingly more expensive to develop, many now choose to do away with the high cost of creating and maintaining internal tools and have switched to the likes of Unity or Unreal. But there are exceptions. Capcom has enjoyed a modern renaissance, powered by its proprietary RE Engine, and now Bandai Namco is boasting about the advantages of its own game engine, using a recent investor Q&A to herald the benefits of this decision.

Bandai Namcoâs engine, called SOL-AVES, is a relatively recent invention at the studio; it was only announced in 2022, although work began on the engine in 2019. During a talk at Yokohama game development conference CEDEC 2026, Bandai Namco spoke about its first public use in Nintendo and Masahiro Sakurai’s co-development of 2026’s Kirby Air Riders. Via a report from Japanese website Game Makers, the engine helped the team in optimizing the project, the game and the engine developed alongside one another. Battling with creating a game that could evoke the sensation of speed, in early development the team struggled to maintain 15 FPS even at a 720p resolution. However, the talk explained how the SOL-AVES engine’s new tricks for lighting and rendering, along with some upscaling, got things running at 60 FPS at 1440p.

The engine was further enhanced during this gameâs development, and now Bandai Namco is confident in its capabilities for future game development. Notably, the company thinks this new engine will be versatile enough to support âa wide range of genres, including fighting games and RPGs.â The Q&A session specifically praised the engineâs processing speed, noting that its rendering speed optimizations were âessential for fighting games.â The engine is, Bandai Namco said, a way to reduce reliance on third-party software while bringing together in-house tools developed by various studios within the company.

Bandai Namco is of course known for its work on the Tales of RPG franchise as well as the Tekken series, heavily implying the SOL-AVES engine will be used to aid future titles in those respective IPs.

Jensen Huang stood down from his role as CEO of Nvidia on November 12. It's November 16 and 175,000…176,000…177,000 people have signed a petition to bring him back. Moreover, it is said the leather-clad man himself is considering a campaign to be reinstated at the helm of Nvidia, and some silicon valley execs are reportedly getting behind him.

There's even a hashtag for the campaign, which feels like a remnant of a lost age when those were actually good for something: #standwithjensen

In an open letter to the Nvidia board, the campaigners ask to "bring Jensen back while an independent investigation establishes the facts, unless and until you can provide compelling evidence that his removal is in Nvidia's best interests."

The Nvidia board has started an investigation into the events that led to Jensen Huang's resignation. If you've been living under a rock, those are: alleged affairs, one of which is said to be with someone suspected of being a Chinese spy, though heavily debated; and questions over smuggling cases and national security risks.

The board has hired legal firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to carry it out under the pretense of it being independent, and Huang had agreed to cooperate with it before his resignation. There's no promise of findings of that investigation being public, however, isn't enough for the signatories of the standwithjensen campaign.

The campaign admits that it cannot verify the roles or affiliations of those claimed to have signed the petition, so take the figures with a pinch of salt; however, it claims nearly 9,000 current employees of Nvidia have signed it, which for a company of just over 40,000, is around 20% of the business. Some big names claimed to have signed the document are Elon Musk, Tim Sweeney (who has been very vocal about his thoughts on the matter), Binance co-founder Yi He, and seemingly many other founders, CEOs, execs, and researchers.

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

Further to this, the Financial Times is reporting that Huang has been discussing the possibility of returning with confidants; presumably not very reliable ones as "people familiar with the matter" are cited in the report, unless they want it to get out, of course. One Huang ally reportedly told the FT it was setting up a "war room" to lobby for the CEO's return and get him back in the good books with US lawmakers.

It wouldn't be an unfamiliar play for a major figure to resign following a scandal with a view to make a return at a later date. Politicians do it regularly enough; UK housing secretary Angela Rayner resigned from Keir Starmer's government following a report that said she broke the Ministerial Code, only to return to the same role under Andy Burnham.

Huang would have a tough path back to leadership. It's not just Nvidia's board that would need convincing, as US lawmakers are set to ask some tough questions of the guy as he joins a few committees in Congress in coming weeks. The outcome of which could either nail shut any chance of return for the ousted CEO, or open the door.

Even if Huang did make it back into the halls of Nvidia's offices, Endeavor and Voyager, in Santa Clara and, one must presume, the leather chair he left in his office, he wouldn't win the prize for shortest leave of absence.

Sam Altman was booted from OpenAI by the board due to a lack of faith in his leadership, and only five days later he was reinstated. Most of OpenAI's employees threatened to resign at the time, though there weren't many of them in total at the time, and a few key people left immediately. That did well to push for his re-hiring, which will surely be something any allies of Huang will have in mind as they build a case for his return.

Steve Jobs was famously ousted from Apple, too, though it took him years to return; he got back when Apple bought his company NeXT, which later went on to form the foundation for every MacBook. So if Huang just builds another company with an even better product, he'll be back in no time.

Nvidia, meanwhile, is reportedly set to be designated one of the United States' "national champions", which the Trump administration is said to be hoping will help win foreign business. Speaking of the US president, Trump had backed Huang before he resigned, but quickly moved on to recommend Apple's Tim Cook as a suitable replacement.

#3739. A new report reckons 40% of developers in the video games industry are using generative AI - but even more think it's harmful

"I did not get into a creative industry to hand over the creativity to an algorithm."

Despite all the outrage and criticism around game developers and publishers using generative AI in gaming, a new report from the Game Developers Conference (GDC) calculates that as many as 40 percent of developers active in the industry use the controversial tools in their work. This is up four percent compared to the same report last year.

That's according to the latest State of the Game Industry report from GDC, which gathers data from more than 2,300 respondents including, but not limited to, game industry professionals, made up of developers, producers, marketers, executives, and investors.

The report notes that 57 percent of developers who say they do use it, use gen-AI for "text generation, research, early prototyping, coding, and presentations". There appears to be a big split between triple-A studios that use gen-AI (with 27 percent of triple-A developers noting that they "feel encouraged or pressured" to use it) and indie devs, of which only nine percent say the same. Perhaps unsurprisingly - given how vocally against gen-AI a lot of 'frontline developers' have been - the tools are mostly used by "business operations and services, mobile-only studios, and free-to-play developers".

There seems to be a gap in the ages of those willing to use AI tools as well; per the report, over half (54 percent) of people 45 years or older reported using the tools - an eight-point increase from last year's survey. There is also more usage among men (45 percent) than women (33 percent).

What is perhaps more striking is that more people responded to the survey saying that they think AI is having a negative impact on games (55 percent) than responded saying they use the tech, suggesting a trend of caution rather than widespread adoption. Notably, respondents saying they are wary of the technology increased one percent since last year, so more people think AI is having a negative effect on the industry now than at the same time in 2025. Perhaps that's because of the sweeping layoffs we've seen across the games industry, often mentioned in the same breath as AI. Or the 'AI slop' that's been flooding Steam and pushing more traditional developers out. Orr some of the abysmal projects we've seen launch that have clearly used gen-AI assets.

"I did not get into a creative industry to hand over the creativity to an algorithm," said one respondent from the UK when explaining why they don't use gen-AI tools. "I got into this industry to collaborate with creative people, not to have an advanced chatbot riff on the ideas of someone who was laid off," said another from California. "I believe that no one should have to read what no human has written and shouldn't have to see what no human has created," said yet another from Minnesota.

The use of generative AI remains controversial in the games industry, though with big companies like Epic and Microsoft doubling down on the tech, it seems this split between developers that want to embrace it and those that don't is only growing larger.

Last night amid the 2026 TV schedule, the 39th Annual Kids' Choice Awards dropped and proved to be quite entertaining. Nominees like Stranger Things, The Thundermans: Undercover, and Spider-Man: Brand New Day triumphantly led the wins this year. And, of course, plenty of people got slimed as is tradition. However, we need to talk about one particular fashion choice that involved an influencer showing up dressed as slime. And I must say, her neon dress is completely bonkers in the best way!

We’ve seen costume fashion before at red carpet events that is incredibly eye-popping. Whether Lady Gaga dressed as meat at the 2010 MTV Video Music Awards or Katy Perry appearing as a hamburger at the 2019 Met Gala, outfits like these certainly keep viewers talking. Speaking of talking, we need to have a chat about influencer Haley Kalil (also known as Haley Baylee) showing up at this year's Kids’ Choice Awards in this slime-colored ensemble:

Now, that’s what you call an eye-popping dress! Although with this one, I'd be afraid to pop anything. The Sports Illustrated Swimsuit Issue winner was sporting a bright green gown with balloons of many different sizes spread throughout. It looks as if the balloons are floating right above her, and this almost feels like a piece someone from Nickelodeon could've curated.

And icing on the cake? Haley Kalil is holding a balloon-like green purse to go with it that says “Win the Mall!”, referencing her upcoming 2026 Netflix competition series. The Miss Minnesota 2014 winner was clearly paying tribute to Nick's history with her unique dress, with the kids' network known for their love of ooey-gooey green slime.

I’m not the only curious mind who needs to know more about this green neon dress. When ET wanted the juice on the creativity that went into making this dress, Kalil gave the credit to a 20-year-old fashion design student named Finn Thompson. She made sure to explain what this unique dress was made of and the secret to putting it together:

[Finn] tied each of these by hand. And the only thing I have on is a bodysuit under this. It’s all made of balloon. Even the back. Even the corset in the back. It’s balloon.

That’s real dedication on the fashion student’s part. It must have taken hours to sew so many balloons onto that bodysuit. The question on my mind is—how does she not pop any of those balloons when she’s sitting down? Fortunately, the Forbes top creator recipient answered that question as well. Here was her response:

I can actually sit because I’m wearing that bodysuit. I just lift up the back, pop a squat. I’m just very wide, you know? So, whoever my chair mate is might have to spare some room on the chairs. Sorry!

So then it’s just a matter of lifting the back of the dress to make sure she’s sitting on the bodysuit. That’s a very smart feature for Thompson to design, to say the least. Otherwise, that would be another way to make heads turn if a loud pop occurred with every squat.

As incredibly bonkers as Haley Kalil’s neon dress is, it’s still a fashion moment that I’m proud to say will live in my mind rent-free. With method dressing being so in right now, there’s no better way to show up at a Nickelodeon event than to make slime look so chic. You can see your favorite movies, TV, and music win big at the 39th Kids’ Choice Awards by streaming now the show with a Paramount+ subscription.

Just your average South Floridian cinephile who believes the pen is mightier than the sword.

#3736. Crimson Desert studio is implementing AI "throughout our entire development pipeline," and expects DokeV to launch in 2028

"This enables a more efficient allocation of development resources and enhances overall production speed."

Crimson Desert and DokeV developer Pearl Abyss is planning to further integrate generative AI into its workflow.

The South Korean studio said as much in its latest quarterly Earnings Letter, explaining that it had previously "validated game systems only after implementing them manually." Now, Pearl Abyss is using AI "to rapidly validate diverse design concepts prior to actual implementation," and argues the move "enables a more efficient allocation of development resources and enhances overall production speed."

"However, AI serves strictly as a tool to support concept validation and pipeline productivity, while the core gameplay experience and actual content creation remain fully driven by our development team," the developer said.

When Crimson Desert first launched, players spotted a crop of suspicious in-game images that looked like they were prompted into existence. Pearl Abyss soon explained that some "2D visual props" were generated with AI tools, but were always intended to be replaced with human-made art, before quickly patching them out of the hit open-world game.

It seems Pearl Abyss is now even more keen on the controversial tech, however: "We are integrating AI technologies to enhance development productivity and overall quality. AI is being utilized across various stages of development - including the automation of repetitive tasks, content creation support, and test optimization - and we are expanding its implementation throughout our entire development pipeline. We view AI not as a substitute for human developers, but as a tool to elevate development efficiency and quality. We will continue to expand our application of AI to deliver higher-fidelity games to the market more expeditiously."

Elsewhere in the letter, the studio said its previously announced creature-collector DokeV is "targeting a launch in the second half of 2028" and we should hear more about it within the year. DokeV was initially targeting a 2023 launch a few years ago. Meanwhile, Crimson Desert is being prepped for a Nintendo Switch 2 launch "in the first half of next year."

The use of generative AI in game development has been a hot topic for years, though it's only become more prevalent in recent months as 'AI slop' floods Steam and big companies like Epic Games proudly adopt the tech. A recent report even estimated that around 40 percent of active developers use AI tools in their work.

The new memory training counter shows your PC hasn't just hung on boot.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Memory training is boring stuff. Your PC will spend an age running through it when you first boot your PC, or you swap in some new RAM sticks (lucky you), or you make a change which has anything to do with memory in your BIOS. Or just because your PC decides it might fancy doing it again. But a new AGESA 1.3.0.1F beta BIOS update, first from Asus (via Uniko's Hardware), has made this whole process a lot more exciting.

Well, going from not at all exciting to something is always going to feel like a bigger deal, but I don't necessarily want to oversell it. Though when you're waiting for memory training to complete it's real nice to at least have a readout to indicate that it is progressing and your PC hasn't just hung.

This is the issue with memory training on PCs in the past. It was pretty damned opaque, in that you'd start up your PC and it would do… nothing. The fans would spin up, and the lights would light, but you'd have no readout on your monitor, and the debug screen on your motherboard would just have a static figure. Mine would be stuck on '15' for an age.

Obviously you could just go looking up the error code and it would inform you that your system was just having a good long think about its system memory, but if you didn't know that could be a thing, it can feel like your rig is bricked.

The new AGESA 1.3.0.1F beta patches are out now, first from Asus, but you can bet other motherboard vendors will be following suit soon enough. This latest version of the AGESA BIOS brings with it AMD's new memory training function, which shows on the motherboard's debug screen that the memory training process is, indeed, proceeding. You'll see it tick up, first from 00 to 09, and then it will go through 0a, 0b, 0c, etc. to show that it is working through the memory training and that it isn't stuck.

You're still getting nothing on your monitor screen, however. The memory training function is done well before your system gets around to turning on your rig's GPU.

My Asus Crosshair X870E Hero board, with 64 GB DDR5-6000, and a Ryzen 9 9950X, went all the way up to 11 (cue guitar riff) before the training was complete and the motherboard rebooted happily.

The PC Gamer Circuit Breaker newsletter breaks down the latest PC gaming tech, and finds you the best deals on the best products

This means you'll immediately see if it is stuck, so no more waiting around for 15 minutes to actually go, 'okay, yeah, this is screwed right here'.

As we've hit the Dave Notes section of this piece, memory training is where your system takes some time to figure out what the best timings and power settings it needs to use in order to get your RAM to run at its preferred speed. This is a periodic thing, and not something that will take place all that often, but when it does, it's slooooooooow.

Your rig will run through voltage/timings combos and validates them alongside test patterns, and then saves its 'best' profile so should be able to always boot reliably at your memory's rated speed. So, on AMD motherboards this is memory training, and why you get a slower than normal boot first time, or when you switch memory. For Intel boards this is called memory refurbishment and is a bit more invisible where it's done in the background.

This latest update is then a pretty small thing for AMD users only, and minor news in the wider world of a reeling tech industry and a market where doing anything to the memory in your rig is almost wishful thinking today, but as a wee quality of life upgrade, and as an AMD CPU user, I'm certainly here for it.

But it's worth noting these are beta BIOS updates, and that comes with some risks that you probably don't need to take in order to get this extra feature. My current official BIOS is AGESA 1.3.0.1d, but I've tested out the new 1.3.0.1f Patch A BIOS from this ROG Forum link. If your rig's running just fine right now, I'd probably suggest sticking with the latest non-beta patches.

Jeopardy! has been one of the best games shows on TV for quite a long time, but I’m rapidly learning it really does take a genius to spell out the show title. The other day, Ken Jennings spoke out about who he feels might be a good fit to step in and take over Jeopardy. The story was pretty widely read on CinemaBlend, and I was honestly kind of appalled to see some of the things people were typing in to get to our page.

In many careers, AI can sometimes be a helpful tool. Other times, it just highlights how bad people are at spelling the word Jeopardy. Thanks to Jeopardy’s current run on the 2026 TV schedule and a little help from AI, I now know the answer is: What is people are awful at it?

Here’s some of the MANY words people type in when it comes to Jeopardy! stories on CinemaBlend, as I saw when I looked in my summary that compiled the search terms people used. Please also note that, yes, all of these were in the Top 20 words people searched when looking for Jeopardy stories on site.

The only thing that gives me a little hope in this world is that the most popular search phrase for Jeopardy on CinemaBlend was in fact “jeopardy.” Yeah, that seems to be lowercase, but who cares? So, thank you to those who, like me, have firmly embedded the correct letter order into their brains. Whether or not you choose to use the exclamation mark feels like a personal choice, and not one to play out in this article.

I do think it’s also worth noting far fewer people type in the more outlandish spellings like “jeperty” than they do “Jeapardy.” The former spelling comes off like, “What accent are we speaking in?” The latter I really feel is people spelling out the show title exactly as it sounds. Regardless, again I’d like to point out these are all Top 20 search terms, so many people still search "jeperty" when looking into what Alex Trebek and co. are up to each week. Let that sit with you for a bit.

Listen, even with Google being significantly more unreliable with search than it has ever been in the company’s history, if you type in “jeperty” (I just did), it will ask if you were intending to search “Jeopardy,” so I see how there’s no real incentive to learn to spell the title of the excellent game show if you haven’t already. You’ll get what you are looking for either way.

I’m just saying though, if you’re invested in a game show series that prides itself on getting trivia facts right (even with the occasional poorly worded clue), maybe as a fan you should invest some time into learning how to spell the show's title?

Jeopardy!’s made some changes over the years, but changing the show’s spelling is probably never going to be one of them. Particularly, if you’re someone who has always wanted to compete on the game show, learning to spell it correctly is a cool thing to do.

#3730. Interest in The Legend of Zelda was "getting smaller and smaller" before Breath of the Wild, according to former Nintendo marketing leads

The Legend of Zelda was in "dire straits" before Breath of the Wild gave the beloved series a massive second wind, according to two former Nintendo marketing leads.

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time's most recent remake has been a mega success, becoming the fastest-selling Switch 2 game so far, but the shiny new adventure has also prompted some online debate over where the series should go next. Should Zelda lean into its carefully directed history - like the one brilliantly remade in Ocarina of Time - or keep the ball rolling with Breath of the Wild's wide open, spontaneous sandbox?

Nintendo of America's ex-director of social media marketing Kit Ellis and former public relations manager Krysta Yang chimed in on the discourse in their latest podcast (below), and explained that Zelda wasn't doing too hot before the Switch era.

"There has been some revisionist history out there lately," Ellis said in response to fans who reckon "the Zelda team ripped away" series staples, like classic dungeons and linear worlds, at the height of their popularity.

"I remember, I was going to the focus groups where it was a really dark moment," Ellis continued. "The feedback was like, 'The fan base is dwindling. This is not bringing in new players.'"

The Legend of Zelda was supposedly "shrinking," while "interest in the audience was getting smaller and smaller" with each new entry. "They had to do something dramatic," Ellis said.

"This series was in dire straits. They were selling, like, nothing," Yang added.

The Zelda series was certainly never irrelevant, but there's a pretty big gap between the roughly 8m copies Twilight Princess sold at the beginning of the Wii generation, the roughly 3m copies Skyward Sword sold at the end of the console's life, and the 34m copies that Breath of the Wild sold just one console generation later.

It was a success so big it spawned a wildly ambitious sequel, Tears of the Kingdom, and even influenced the latest 2D Zelda, Echoes of Wisdom. Now that classic Zelda's back in the spotlight, though, I do hope Nintendo's able to slot the series' curated dungeons into whatever the next mainline game becomes.
